scope: Offline follow-up assistant knowledge for the Plant Doctor classifier. It supports care guidance, prevention, spread, watering, monitoring, and safety limitations. It does not replace local agricultural advice or product labels.

symptoms: Small water-soaked spots become dark brown.
Yellow halos may appear around spots.
Severe infection can merge spots and blight leaves.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.cause: Xanthomonas bacteria are favored by wet leaves, rain splash, wind-driven rain, contaminated seed, and contaminated tools.
watering: Water early enough that foliage dries quickly.
organic: Remove infected leaves or plants and destroy them.
Use certified disease-free seed or transplants.
Copper products may be used where labels permit, but resistance and crop injury are possible.
chemical: Copper-based bactericides are commonly used as protectants.
Follow the product label and local agricultural guidance.
Do not invent dosage or harvest interval.
prevention: Rotate away from tomato, pepper, and related crops for at least two years.
Avoid saving seed from infected plants.
spread: Can spread by splashing water, wind-driven rain, tools, hands, and infected plant debris.
Remove badly infected material and avoid working in wet plants.
monitoring: Check new growth every few days after rain.
Watch for new water-soaked spots and yellow halos.
Escalate if defoliation begins.

symptoms: Older lower leaves show dark brown spots.
Spots often form concentric target-like rings.
Yellowing around lesions can progress upward.
Tomato_Early_blight.cause: Alternaria solani survives in crop debris and is favored by warm humid conditions and leaf wetness.
watering: Avoid wetting leaves late in the day.
organic: Keep plants evenly watered and avoid stress.
chemical: Protectant fungicides such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb may be used where labelled.
Follow the label for rate, timing, protective equipment, and harvest interval.
prevention: Maintain plant spacing and balanced fertility.
spread: Spores move from debris and lower leaves by splash and wind.
Bag and discard infected leaves instead of leaving them on soil.
monitoring: Inspect lower leaves twice weekly in humid weather.
Act early before spots move high into the canopy.

symptoms: Large greasy gray-green water-soaked patches can appear on leaves or stems.
White mold may appear on leaf undersides in humid conditions.
Plants can collapse rapidly.
Tomato_Late_blight.cause: Phytophthora infestans spreads quickly in cool wet weather and prolonged leaf wetness.
conditions: Nearby infected tomato or potato plants
watering: Keep foliage as dry as possible.
Do not work among wet plants.
organic: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately.
Improve airflow and reduce leaf wetness.
chemical: Late blight often requires preventive fungicide programs guided by local disease forecasts.
Products such as mancozeb or metalaxyl combinations must be used only according to label and local advice.
prevention: Destroy volunteer tomato and potato plants.
Remove infected debris at season end.
spread: Can spread quickly by windborne spores and infected plant debris.
Separate suspect plants and remove severely infected plants quickly.
monitoring: Inspect daily during cool wet periods.
Urgent expert guidance is recommended because this disease can destroy plants quickly.

symptoms: Upper leaf surfaces show pale green or yellow patches.
Olive-brown velvety mold appears on undersides.
Leaves may curl, wither, and drop.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.cause: Passalora fulva thrives when humidity is high and ventilation is poor, especially in protected cultivation.
chemical: Copper fungicides or chlorothalonil may be labelled in some areas.
Use only label-approved products and intervals.
spread: Spores spread in humid air and on plant debris.
Remove infected leaves and avoid brushing wet foliage.
monitoring: Check undersides of leaves for velvety mold.
Watch humidity and airflow after irrigation.

symptoms: Many small circular spots form on leaves.
Spots often have dark borders and pale gray centers.
Tiny black fruiting bodies may be visible in spot centers.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.cause: Septoria lycopersici survives in debris and spreads in warm wet conditions by splash.
watering: Avoid splashing water onto lower leaves.
organic: Discard infected debris away from the garden.
chemical: Mancozeb or chlorothalonil may be used where labelled.
Follow local label directions and pre-harvest intervals.
spread: Spreads mainly by splashing water from infected debris and lower leaves.
Bag infected leaves and keep the soil surface clean.
monitoring: Scout after rain.
Act when spots are still mostly on lower leaves.

symptoms: Leaves show tiny yellow or bronze stippling.
Fine webbing may appear on undersides.
Leaves can yellow, dry, and drop.
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.cause: Two-spotted spider mites increase rapidly in hot dry dusty conditions, especially on stressed plants.
watering: A strong water spray can help dislodge mites, but avoid prolonged leaf wetness in disease-prone conditions.
organic: Spray leaf undersides with water to dislodge mites.
Use insecticidal soap or neem oil where labelled.
Encourage or release predatory mites when appropriate.
chemical: Use a labelled miticide for heavy infestations only after confirming mites.
Rotate modes of action according to expert guidance and label.
spread: Mites move plant to plant and can be carried by wind or handling.
Separate badly infested plants if practical.
monitoring: Check undersides with a hand lens.
Look for moving mites and webbing every few days in hot weather.

symptoms: Brown lesions may show concentric rings.
Leaves, stems, and fruit can be affected.
Severe cases can cause defoliation.
Tomato__Target_Spot.cause: Corynespora cassiicola is favored by high humidity, warm weather, and dense foliage.
watering: Improve drying through spacing and pruning.
chemical: Azoxystrobin or chlorothalonil may be labelled in some regions.
Follow label directions and local resistance-management advice.
spread: Spores spread from infected tissue in humid conditions.
Remove infected leaves and reduce leaf wetness.
monitoring: Inspect leaves and fruit for expanding ringed lesions.
Treat early when local guidance supports it.

symptoms: Young leaves curl upward and yellow.
Plants may become stunted.
Flower drop and poor fruit set can occur.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.cause: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus is spread mainly by whiteflies.
conditions: Warm regions with continuous host plants
watering: Watering does not cure the virus.
Avoid plant stress while managing whiteflies.
organic: Use yellow sticky traps for monitoring.
Exclude whiteflies with fine mesh where feasible.
chemical: Whitefly insecticides may be labelled, but product choice must follow local guidance and resistance management.
No chemical cures infected plants.
prevention: Remove crop weeds and infected plants.
spread: Whiteflies carry the virus between plants.
Removing infected plants reduces virus sources but does not cure exposed plants.
monitoring: Monitor new growth and whitefly numbers.
Use sticky traps and inspect leaf undersides.

symptoms: Leaves show light and dark green mosaic patterns.
Leaves may be distorted, narrow, or fern-like.
Fruit may show yellow blotches.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: Tomato mosaic virus spreads by contact through hands, tools, clothing, seed, or infected plant material.
watering: Watering does not cure viral infection.
Avoid handling wet plants because contact can spread sap.
chemical: No chemical treatment cures mosaic virus.
Do not apply pesticides expecting to cure infected plants.
prevention: Use resistant varieties and clean seed.
Avoid tobacco contact before working with tomatoes.
spread: Spreads by physical contact and contaminated tools.
Handle suspect plants last and sanitize afterward.
monitoring: Watch new leaves for mosaic patterns and distortion.
Remove confirmed infected plants quickly.

symptoms: No clear disease symptoms detected by the classifier.
Tomato_healthy.cause: No disease cause is indicated by this result.
conditions: Healthy plants can still develop disease after weather changes or pest movement.
watering: Water at soil level where possible.
chemical: Do not apply chemical treatment without symptoms or local expert guidance.
spread: No disease spread is indicated by a healthy result.
monitoring: Retake a photo if spots, curling, mold, stippling, or rapid yellowing appear.
